title: Everything you need to start preparing for case interviews, in the order to learn it
description: Everything you need to start preparing for case interviews, in order: how cases work, the ten stages, frameworks, maths, sizing, fit and a study plan.
hook: If you are new to case interviews, everything can feel like a lot at once: frameworks, maths, charts, fit questions, and a whole new vocabulary. This guide puts it in order. Read it once from top to bottom and you will know what a case is, how it flows, what to practise, and where to go next on this blog.
body:
What a case interview is

A case interview is a conversation, usually 20 to 40 minutes, about a real-feeling business problem. You are not expected to know the answer. You are expected to break the problem down, use numbers sensibly, and reach a clear recommendation, all while talking the interviewer through your thinking. Read the full explanation.

How a case flows, in ten stages

  1. Listen and take notes: Everything later links back to the goal you write down now.
  2. Recap: Shows you listened, and checks you are solving the right problem.
  3. Clarifying questions (three at most): The right question can split the whole case in two before you draw anything.
  4. Structure: Interviewers weigh it heavily. Your structure is your plan for the whole case.
  5. Lead the case: Interviewers score whether you drive. Waiting to be told what to do loses candidate-led cases.
  6. Charts and exhibits: Exhibits test whether you can find what matters, and many cases turn on them.
  7. Maths: Numbers turn opinions into evidence. Errors under pressure are the most common confidence killer.
  8. Brainstorm: Even open questions are structuring questions in disguise.
  9. Recommendation: The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers and writes up.
  10. Throughout the case: You are being judged on how you come across in every minute, not just the answers.

The course, in order

If you want to learn properly, work through these eleven guides in order. Each takes about ten minutes.

  1. How case interviews work. What a case interview is, the two formats you will meet, and the six things every interviewer scores.
  2. The opening: listen, recap, clarify. The first three minutes set the tone. How to take notes, recap without repeating, and ask questions that actually help.
  3. Structuring: issue trees and hypotheses. The most heavily weighted skill. How to build a MECE structure for any problem, and why you must say where you would start.
  4. Driving the case. In candidate-led cases you are expected to steer, and even in interviewer-led ones, proposing next steps earns credit. Summarise as you go, and keep linking back to the goal.
  5. Case maths without the panic. The arithmetic is simple; doing it out loud under pressure is not. Approach first, round smartly, sanity-check everything.
  6. Reading charts and exhibits. Exhibits are where cases are won or lost. A five-step routine for turning any chart into an insight.
  7. Market sizing. How many, how big, how much. The structure earns the points, not the final number.
  8. Brainstorming with structure. "What could the client do?" is still a structuring question. Use buckets, not a list.
  9. The recommendation. The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers. Answer first, reasons with numbers, risks, next steps.
  10. How you come across. The half of the interview most candidates never train: voice, composure and business fluency.
  11. The fit interview. Behavioural questions often count as much as the case. Build 6-8 stories once, and use each for several questions.

Frameworks, without the memorising

Most cases fall into three families: diagnosing a problem, deciding yes or no, or generating options. Here is how to tell which one you are in, and the eleven core frameworks that cover nearly every case.

Maths, charts and sizing

The case maths cheat sheet has everything on one page. For estimation questions, start with the market sizing guide and then try twenty-four worked examples.

The fit interview

Half of most consulting interviews is about you. Here are the questions you will be asked, and how to build stories that answer them.

outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case.
